prompt.context: Our client is a for-profit, specialty college named Chic Cosmetology University (CCU). Founded in 2005, CCU is a program for high school graduates seeking their professional cosmetology license. CCU is currently the market leader for cosmetology education with campuses in ten major metropolitan areas in the US. CCU has capital to invest in a new campus and is considering Chicagoland as a location.
prompt.question: Should CCU open a new campus in Chicagoland?

clarifying_info.q: What does CCU consider a successful launch?
clarifying_info.a: The client considers a successful launch as achieving positive operating profit for the new campus two years after opening.

clarifying_info.q: How long do enrolled students take classes? What is the program structure?
clarifying_info.a: Enrolled students take classes at a physical campus for one school year to earn their degree. The fiscal year begins on September 1.

clarifying_info.q: What is CCU's competitive position / quality?
clarifying_info.a: CCU boasts the best campuses in the industry with state-of-the-art equipment and strong job placement due to relationships with top salons in local areas.

clarifying_info.q: How fast is the market growing?
clarifying_info.a: CCU and industry enrollments are growing at 5% per year.

There are 2-3 other large specialty colleges, some of which are in the same geographies as CCU. Community colleges are also beginning to offer cosmetology degrees at lower prices. All ten CCU campuses and all competitor campuses have been present for at least three full school years.

clarifying_info.q: What are the industry requirements to become a cosmetologist?
clarifying_info.a: A high school diploma and a cosmetology degree are required to enter the field. 98% of cosmetologists are women.

clarifying_info.q: What is the investment cost of opening a new campus in Chicagoland?
clarifying_info.a: The total cost is $4.5M in initial building costs to renovate the chosen site. These costs can be amortized evenly over a three-year period. Assume fixed costs remain flat per year.

exhibits.title: 2010 CCU Financials
exhibits.shows: A financial summary table for CCU as of 8/31/2010, showing system-wide student enrollments, revenues, fixed campus costs broken into subcategories, variable campus costs broken into subcategories, and operating profit. All figures are in thousands of dollars.

exhibits.title: CCU and Major Competitor Campus Locations
exhibits.shows: A table listing CCU campus cities and their 2010 market share (measured as share of total potential students as defined by CCU), alongside a map showing the locations of CCU campuses and major competitor campuses across the US as of 8/31/2010.

data.note: CCU campus and major competitor campus icons shown on map

framework: 1. Evaluate CCU revenue and cost structure (revenue per student, fixed cost per campus, variable cost per student, gross profit per student)
2. Determine break-even enrollment for the new Chicago campus (include amortization of initial investment)
3. Estimate the total addressable market in Chicagoland (targeted high schools + adult market)
4. Project CCU's realistic market share in Chicago based on competitive dynamics
5. Compare projected Year 1 enrollment to break-even enrollment
6. Identify qualitative factors and strategic alternatives

questions.prompt: What is the average revenue per enrollment, fixed cost per campus, variable cost per student, and gross profit per student?
questions.guidance: Candidate should derive per-unit economics from the system-wide Exhibit 1 figures by dividing by 10 campuses or 10,000 enrollments. Revenue per enrollment = $15K; fixed cost per campus = $4.8M; variable cost per student = $8K; gross profit per student = $7K.

math.setup: All figures from Exhibit 1. Divide system totals by 10 campuses or 10,000 total enrollments.
steps: Total annual fixed cost per campus = $48,000K / 10 campuses = $4,800K = $4.8M
Total variable cost per student = $80,000K / 10,000 students = $8K
math.answer: Revenue per student: $15K; Fixed cost per campus: $4.8M; Variable cost per student: $8K; Gross profit per student: $7K

questions.prompt: What is the break-even number of students required for the new CCU Chicago campus in Year 1?
questions.guidance: Candidate must ask about the investment cost of the new campus and factor in yearly amortization. Total fixed cost = standing fixed cost + amortization. Break-even = total fixed cost / gross profit per student. Answer is 900 students.

math.setup: Initial building cost = $4.5M amortized evenly over 3 years. Annual amortization = $1.5M. Total annual fixed cost = $4.8M + $1.5M = $6.3M. Break-even = total fixed cost / gross profit per student.

questions.prompt: What types of schools and students do you think CCU targets, and how many students could CCU Chicago expect to enroll in Year 1 at most?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify the target profile (women HS graduates not attending 4-year college, from public/middle-class HS near campus), then use the provided data on 1,000 targeted HS with 6 potential students each and the adult market multiplier. Total potential HS students = 6,000; adult market = 1,500 (20% of total enrolled come from adult market, so adult potential = 6,000 * 25% = 1,500). Total potential = 7,500. At 10% market share (justified from Exhibit 2: cities with one competitor average ~10%), Year 1 enrollment = 750. Year 2 = 788 (applying 5% growth).

math.setup: CCU has identified 1,000 targeted high schools in Chicagoland. On average 6 students per HS have potential for CCU enrollment. 80% of enrolled students come directly from HS, 20% from the adult market. Projected market share for Chicago (one competitor present) = 10%.
steps: Potential HS students = 6 students/HS x 1,000 HS = 6,000 students
Adult market: HS = 80% of total, Adult = 20% of total, so Adult potential = 6,000 * (20/80) = 6,000 * 25% = 1,500 students
Year 1 enrollment at 10% share = 7,500 x 10% = 750 students
math.answer: 750 students in Year 1; 788 students in Year 2

questions.prompt: (Bonus, if time permits) Suppose CCU finds a lot with a one-time construction cost of $300K with the same amortization schedule. Should they enter Chicago now?
questions.guidance: Candidate recalculates break-even with the lower amortization. New break-even = 700 students. However, an excellent candidate should note that the 10% market share benchmark is for campuses present for at least 3 full school years — Chicago is unlikely to achieve that share in Year 1 or 2. Therefore even a lower investment does not clearly make entry feasible in the near term.

math.setup: New one-time cost = $300K amortized over 3 years. New annual amortization = $100K.
steps: 750 > 700, so on paper break-even is achievable — BUT the 10% market share is a mature-campus benchmark (3+ years), so Year 1 actual share is likely lower, making 750 an optimistic ceiling
math.answer: Break-even drops to 700 students; projected Year 1 enrollment of 750 would nominally exceed break-even, but the market share assumption is aggressive for a new campus and feasibility remains questionable

brainstorming.prompt: What types of schools and students should CCU target for enrollment in Chicagoland?

categories.name: Target Schools
ideas: Public high schools (private HS graduates more likely to attend 4-year universities)
High schools in middle-class neighborhoods (affordability concern with very low-income areas)
High schools geographically closest to the campus

categories.name: Target Students
ideas: Women high school graduates (98% of cosmetologists are women)
Graduates not planning to attend a 4-year college
Students with demonstrated interest in cosmetology or beauty
Adult market — women who did not go directly from HS to a cosmetology program

recommendation: CCU should NOT enter the Chicago market under the current cost structure
Even under the most optimistic assumptions (10% market share), Year 1 enrollment of 750 students falls 150 students short of the 900 required to break even
The 10% market share benchmark is based on mature campuses with 3+ years of presence, so Year 1 reality is likely worse than projected
risks: Actual Year 1 market share will likely be below 10% since the benchmark applies to established campuses (3+ years), meaning enrollment shortfall could be larger than 150 students
Community college competition at lower price points could compress CCU's share further
If growth rate of 5% holds, Year 2 projects only 788 students — still short of the 900 break-even target
next_steps: Consider offering scholarships to increase the number of potential students and/or improve conversion rate of potential students
Evaluate other cities beyond Chicagoland that currently have no CCU presence, or add a second campus to a high-share city like NYC
Conduct market research in other cities to identify locations with greater potential per target high school
Identify ways to reduce fixed costs, e.g., transporting equipment and materials from campuses that are not at full capacity
